To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the prefrontal and parietal cortex are involved in the control of memory retrieval in humans, and 2) this control involves a top-down modulation of the retrieval process.
(1) there is evidence that there are multiple memory systems in the brain and (2) there is evidence for mechanisms by which a particular memory system gains control over behavior.
(1) the prefrontal and hippocampal systems are involved in learning and memory, and (2) the prefrontl and hippocampal system interact to influence learning and memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the brain controls learning and memory.
understanding the mechanisms by which the mammalian brain controls behavior.
the mechanisms that influence the control of learning and memory systems over voluntary behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanisms that determine which learning and memory system controls behavior are complex and not well understood at this time.

we are not yet ready to make definitive statements about how different learning and memory processes interact to influence behavior, and we do not know how the brain mediates the interactions of these systems to control behavior.
there are multiple systems that can control learning and memory and the system that gains control depends on a variety of factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a number of factors that might contribute to the control of behavior by different memory systems in different contexts.
there are many ways that a learning and memory can gain control of behavior and these processes can be influenced by both external factors and brain factors.
the hippocampus is not a single system, but rather a collection of functionally distinct subsystems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain has multiple systems that mediate learning and memory.
the organization of learning in the mammalian central nervous system is more complex and dynamic than previously appreciated.
we have identified a set of processes that might be involved in the control of behavior.
